analysis.one_liner: Makes generic drug makers pay Medicaid extra rebates when their prices rise faster than inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill to make generic drug makers pay Medicaid rebates when prices outpace inflation was referred to committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current Medicaid law, brand-name drug manufacturers must pay states an extra rebate if their prices rise faster than inflation, but generic drug makers do not. This bill would close that gap, requiring generic manufacturers to pay the same inflation penalty when they raise prices. Generic drugs make up most Medicaid prescriptions, so the bill targeted rising generic prices that have been driving up costs for the program that covers low-income Americans. It was introduced late in the 113th Congress and died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: State Medicaid programs and taxpayers would gain, because the inflation-penalty rebates would claw back money when generic prices spike. The 70 million or so Americans covered by Medicaid, most of them low-income families, children, seniors, and people with disabilities, would benefit from reduced program cost pressure and slower price increases on their medicines.

how_it_helps.text: It extends the Medicaid 'additional rebate'—an extra payment manufacturers owe when a drug's price rises faster than inflation—to generic drugs, which are currently excluded.
State Medicaid programs would collect the additional rebates, reducing public spending or offsetting costs in a program that covers low-income Americans.

analysis.who_pays: Generic drug manufacturers would pay the additional rebates whenever their Medicaid prices rise faster than inflation. Any cost pressure could be passed into prices for other purchasers, and manufacturers could reduce discounts elsewhere to offset the rebate.

drawbacks.text: Generic drugs are typically the cheapest option, and additional mandatory rebates could reduce generic manufacturers' margins, which in a thin-margin industry could discourage some firms from staying in markets for low-volume Medicaid drugs.

The rebate applies whenever a generic price rises faster than inflation, without regard to whether the price rise reflects genuine increases in the cost of making the drug, so manufacturers would bear the rebate even when inflation in their own inputs drove the increase.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—slower price growth for a program covering low-income Americans—would come at a real but limited cost to generic makers, who are generally lower-margin than brand-name companies and might respond with slightly higher launch prices or fewer products. The design is simple and targeted at a documented gap in existing law, and the mechanism (inflation-linked rebates) was already in place for brand-name drugs, so it would not create a new administrative system.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and no vote or further action ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House introduced the bill on November 20, 2014 and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
The next day it was referred to the committee's Health Subcommittee, where it stayed.
With the 113th Congress ending on January 3, 2015, the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and all pending legislation died when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Generic drug manufacturers benefit because they will not owe extra Medicaid rebates when their prices rise faster than inflation, and the committee members who never scheduled action preserved that status quo.

for.name: Rep. Elijah E. Cummings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the Medicaid inflation rebate to generic drug manufacturers.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicaid drug pricing
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its referral to the Health Subcommittee, so it never advanced.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: The pharmaceutical industry consistently opposed expanding Medicaid rebate obligations, lobbying heavily on drug pricing bills during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members were involved, both Democrats, so the record shows no test of how the parties would have split; the bill died before any vote could reveal it.

industries.note: The bill would require generic makers to pay an extra Medicaid rebate whenever their prices rise faster than inflation, a requirement that currently applies only to brand-name drugs. Generic makers are the bill's direct target.

Brand-name makers already pay the inflation rebate; the bill would not change their obligations directly, but it would remove a competitive advantage generics currently have under Medicaid pricing rules, tightening the market they sell into.

The bill's purpose is to save money for Medicaid, the government program covering low-income patients, by collecting rebates when generic prices spike. The savings would fall on the public side of the ledger as a gain.
